summary.text: When Jupiter and Mercury wandered Phrygia in mortal guise and a thousand doors closed against them, one humble cottage opened — Baucis and Philemon, poor, old, and content, shared their last goose and their hearth with the gods; the valley flooded, only their roof was spared, and at life's end they became an intertwining oak and linden guarding the temple that rose on the spot.

chapters.title: The wanderers
chapters.text: After the Calydonian boar and the tales of Daedalus, Ovid turns to Phrygia, where the gods often tested mortals. Jupiter and Mercury came down without their insignia and knocked at a thousand houses; every door stayed shut until they reached a small thatched cottage on the slope, where an old couple greeted them as equals.

chapters.title: Humble hospitality
chapters.text: Baucis and Philemon had grown old together in the same cottage where they married as youths; they owned little but shared it freely — a couch, a table, olives, garden greens, and a goose they chased round the room until the gods forbade the sacrifice. The wine bowl refilled itself; the couple wept to see divine power in their poor house and prayed forgiveness for having no better fare.

chapters.title: The flood
chapters.text: Jupiter revealed himself and led them up the hill; the valley below became a marsh, and every proud house sank — only Baucis and Philemon's cottage stood, and as they watched it turned into a temple with marble columns and a golden roof. The gods asked what reward they wished; the pair asked only to die together, serving the temple as priest and priestess.

chapters.title: Oak and linden
chapters.text: Years later, tending the shrine, they saw each other sprouting leaves — bark covered their limbs, and they merged into an oak and a linden with intertwining branches. A latticed screen still guarded the spot in Ovid's day, and garlands hung on the boughs that had been faithful Philemon and pious Baucis.
